title: No append verb: every 'add a note to this task' is a hand-built read-modify-write, and it has destroyed or silently no-opped at least six task bodies across seven weeks

body:
Filed 2026-08-23 from the Enix side, where trk is used heavily by agents. Scott's suggestion, and the
evidence for it is stronger than "it would be convenient".

## THE GAP

`trk edit <id> --body` REPLACES. There is no append. So the universal operation "add a note to this
task" is a hand-built read-modify-write performed by the CALLER, in shell, every time.

## WHY THAT IS THE WRONG PLACE FOR IT -- the load-bearing argument

**Only trk can read its own body correctly.** The current body is the merge of `log.jsonl`'s setBody
events AND `snapshot.jsonl` -- `trk compact` writes a full-state snapshot and TRUNCATES the log, so a
body last written before the most recent compact lives in the snapshot and NOWHERE ELSE. Every
external append helper has to reimplement that merge, and there is a recorded instance of one getting
it wrong destructively: a helper scanning only `log.jsonl` for the last setBody returned "0 existing
chars" for such a task, the caller wrote existing+addition, and the task lost its ENTIRE original
body. It hit TWICE in one session (Enix rows 01KVKJ1EN, 01KXMMVK5).

An append verb deletes the reconstruction step. The tool already knows how to read its own state; the
caller does not, and cannot be expected to.

## MEASURED HISTORY -- six instances, seven weeks, all one root cause

  2026-07-03  backticks inside a double-quoted `--body` ran as SHELL; the stored body had HOLES where
              the backticked words were.
  2026-08-07  the compact/snapshot case above -- helper reported "0 existing", caller TRUNCATED. x2.
  2026-08-13  a shell-substituted "old body + append" with a silent `|| echo ''` fallback WIPED a
              row's whole diagnosis trail (Enix 01KZY98VM); recovered only because the old text
              happened to still be in the agent's context.
  2026-08-20  compact/merge silently dropped a live task's most-recent setBody (01KZTV44M) -- adjacent
              cause, same blast radius, and the recovery was again a hand re-apply of extracted bytes.
  2026-08-21  two separate "re-verified, appended" commits on 01KZ3BW22 wrote BYTE-IDENTICAL bodies.
              Zero durable signal added, no error, no warning. The task kept getting re-worked
              because each pass silently overwrote the last.
  (+ this repo's own 01M0EM10X: "an agent lost a multi-paragraph body to this".)

Two of trk's own issues have ALREADY been closed against symptoms of this gap -- 01KXC1TY5 added
`show --body` as "a raw body read path for safe edit round-trips", and 01M0EM10X made `--body -` read
stdin instead of storing the literal "-". Both made the MANUAL round-trip safer. Neither removed the
need to do it manually, and the losses continued after both landed. That is the argument for fixing
the primitive rather than the third symptom.

Corroborating signal on frequency: the consuming project documents the workaround in THREE separate
runbooks and ships a shim script (`scripts/trk-note.sh`) whose entire purpose is to wrap this. A
one-off does not get written into three runbooks.

## PROPOSED SHAPE (not prescriptive -- the maintainer's call)

1. **`trk note <id> <text>`** (or `trk append`) -- read the current body via trk's own state merge,
   append, write. Accepts `-` for stdin like `--body` now does, so long text needs no shell quoting.
   Optionally a separator convention (blank line, or a `--sep` flag).
2. **Keep `--body` as REPLACE**, unchanged and explicit. The two operations are genuinely different
   and both are wanted; the bug is that only one is spellable.
3. **Consider making a byte-identical setBody loud** -- a warning, or a `--allow-noop`. That is the
   2026-08-21 case: the write "succeeded" while adding nothing, and the silence is what let it repeat.
4. Possibly `--body-file <path>` as a third spelling, since agents already stage bodies in files to
   dodge shell quoting.

## WHY IT MATTERS DISPROPORTIONATELY HERE

trk's value is accumulated context -- a task body that grows a diagnosis trail across sessions is the
whole point of an append-only tracker. This gap attacks exactly that: every loss above destroyed
accumulated reasoning, and the 2026-08-21 case destroyed it invisibly, so the task read as
"investigated twice" while holding one pass's worth of content. A tracker whose append operation can
silently truncate is failing at its defining job.

Restated as the mandate this project applies to its own kernel APIs: `--body` is a footgun whose

since the workaround is already documented in three runbooks plus a shim script and the losses
continued anyway.

### One addition, and it is the load-bearing half of the migration

**REMOVE `--body` outright; do not deprecate it.** A deprecation that still performs the replace
preserves the exact failure mode for every existing caller — the warning scrolls past in an agent's

annotating them.

Note trk already has a deprecation precedent and it is instructive by contrast: `--add-tag arc:<slug>`
is "still honored, but warns". That is correct THERE, because the legacy behaviour is harmless — the
tag lands, just via the old spelling. Honor-with-warning is the wrong instrument here, where honoring
the old spelling IS the bug.

The blast radius is small and known: the consuming project's `scripts/trk-note.sh`, three runbook
mentions, and agent prompts — all mechanical, all one-time, all better fixed loudly than left to fail
silently one more time.

title: Mutation verbs are inconsistently invertible: --add-tag/--rm-tag pair, dep/undep pair, but --add-doc has NO removal and a typo'd doc-ref is permanent short of hand-editing .tracker

body:
Filed 2026-08-23 from the Enix side. Sibling of 01M0QJ8K4 (the missing body-append verb) and the same
underlying shape: a mutation exists in one direction only, so the recovery path is hand-editing
.tracker/ -- which every consuming runbook forbids as the cardinal sin.

VERIFIED AT HEAD (not relayed from the originating finding, which is from 2026-07-21 and predates
several trk upgrades):
    trk edit --help  |  grep --rm-doc  ->  0 hits.  There is no removal flag.
Confirmed still-live. The originating symptom: `trk edit <id> --add-doc <bad-id>` permanently attaches
a doc-ref; `--rm-doc` is an unknown flag. A typo'd or placeholder doc id (e.g. "none") becomes a
permanent cosmetic doc-ref. Harmless in effect -- it points nowhere -- but uneditable except by a raw
log edit, which is exactly the operation the tool's own consumers are told never to perform.

THE INCONSISTENCY IS INTERNAL, which is what makes it a defect rather than a wish:
    --add-tag / --rm-tag     PAIRED
    dep       / undep        PAIRED (and `dep --help` explicitly points at undep as the fix)
    doc set   / doc unset    PAIRED (01KXC1TY7, landed)
    --add-doc / (nothing)    UNPAIRED   <-- this issue
    --body    / (nothing)    UNPAIRED   <-- 01M0QJ8K4, now ruled
The tool has already decided, four times, that a mutation gets an inverse. Two escaped.

NOTE the distinction from 01KXC1TY7, which is DONE and is a different verb: `trk doc unset` removes a
doc_id -> path REGISTRATION. This is about removing a doc-REF from a TASK. Registering correctly does
not help a task that already carries a bad ref.

PROPOSED: `--rm-doc <doc_id>` on `trk edit`, mirroring `--rm-tag` exactly (tombstoned, union-merge-safe,
same as the existing removal verbs). If a doc-ref should be immutable by design, say so in `edit --help`
and the recovery guidance -- but silence plus an unknown-flag error reads as an oversight, and the
consumer's only remaining route is the forbidden one.

WORTH AUDITING WHILE IN THERE: whether any other mutation is one-directional. The two found here were
found by asking the question, not by hitting them -- 01M0QJ8K4 cost six task bodies before anyone asked.

title: archive buries any DECISION living in a closing task's body — archived is hidden from every view, so a 'FIX NOTE' / open fork / 'your call' section is graduated out of sight with the work

body:
Filed 2026-08-23 from the Enix side, where the workaround is documented in two runbooks and has still
cost a measured loss.

VERIFIED AT HEAD: `trk archive --help` mentions nothing about decisions or open questions (grep for
decision/open question -> 0 hits). The behaviour is as designed; the hazard is that the design has a
sharp edge nobody is warned about at the point of use.

THE HAZARD. `archive` graduates the done queue to the changelog and flips each task to `archived`,
which is a TOMBSTONE hidden from every view. A task body, however, routinely accumulates more than the
work: a "FIX NOTE", an open fork, a "this part is Scott's call", an OPEN QUESTION. The WORK was done --
the task is legitimately closeable -- but the DECISION was never that task's scope, and archiving takes
it out of sight along with the tombstone.

MEASURED: on 2026-08-12 a publish-cadence fork was archived out of sight this way and recovered only by
accident while someone wrote a handoff. The consuming project now carries the mitigation in two
runbooks as a manual pre-archive step: grep the done queue's bodies for `scott-decision` / `OPEN
QUESTION` / `FIX NOTE` / `your call` and `trk add` each as a standalone task BEFORE archiving. That
mitigation is prose, it fires only if the operator remembers, and it is duplicated in two places --
the same shape as 01M0QJ8K4's three-runbook workaround, which kept failing until the primitive changed.

WHY THE TOOL IS THE RIGHT PLACE. `archive` already walks every body it is about to graduate -- it emits
a changelog bullet per task. It is the only actor that sees the full done queue at the moment of
burial, and it is the only one that can act before the tombstone hides the text.

PROPOSED SHAPES, unweighed:
  (a) `archive` scans each closing body for a configurable marker set (default: `scott-decision`,
      `OPEN QUESTION`, `FIX NOTE`, `your call`, `TODO`) and WARNS, listing task id + matched line, so
      the operator can split them out first. Non-blocking; the warning is the whole value.
  (b) as (a) but REFUSES without `--allow-buried-decisions`, on the grounds that this is a data-loss
      class and a warning in a long archive run scrolls past (the same argument that ruled hard-removal
      over deprecation on 01M0QJ8K4).
  (c) `archive --dry-run` -- which already exists and previews the queue -- additionally reports the
      marker hits, making the existing preview step sufficient without changing archive's own contract.

(c) is the cheapest and composes with the existing workflow; (b) is the strongest if this is judged a
data-loss class rather than an ergonomics one. Maintainer's call.

NOT A BUG in the merge/tombstone model -- `archived` hiding from every view is correct and deliberate.
This is about what rides along with it.

title: dep/undep take two bare positionals whose order silently inverts the edge — make the direction explicit: trk dep <id> --needs <id>

body:
Filed 2026-08-23 from the Enix side. Third of the explicit-direction family, with 01M0QJ8K4 (body
replace/append, RULED) and 01M0QK1C4 (--add-doc has no inverse).

THE SHAPE. `trk dep A B` means "A needs B". Both arguments are bare positionals of the same type, so
reversing them produces a VALID edge pointing the wrong way — the DAG is wrong, the ready frontier is
wrong, and nothing errors.

PROPOSED: `trk dep <id> --needs <id>`, and `trk undep <id> --needs <id>` to match. ONE positional, ONE
flagged. The asymmetry is the mechanism: you cannot SWAP two things when only one of them is spellable
positionally, so a reversal stops being a typo and becomes a sentence you would have to write
backwards deliberately. It also reads as one: `trk dep 01ABC --needs 01XYZ`.

REJECTED ALTERNATIVES, so they are not re-proposed:
  * BOTH flagged (`--needer X --prereq Y`) — order-independent, but you still have to know which word
    means which, so it moves the confusion from position to vocabulary rather than removing it. And
    "needer" is not a word anyone reaches for.
  * INFIX keyword (`trk dep A needs B`) — reads best of the three, but it is an unusual CLI shape,
    undiscoverable from --help conventions, and inconsistent with trk's otherwise flag-based surface
    (--add-tag, --rm-tag, --priority).

MIGRATION: hard-error the bare two-positional form rather than accepting both, on the same reasoning
Scott ruled for 01M0QJ8K4 — a tolerated legacy spelling keeps the footgun, and here the blast radius is
small and known (CLAUDE.md's tracker section, a few runbook lines, agent prompt boilerplate).

=== SEVERITY, STATED HONESTLY — this is POLISH, not a defect, and should rank BELOW 01M0QJ8K4 and
01M0QK25Q ===

Unlike the body-append gap, this one is well-mitigated at HEAD and I could find no measured instance in
the Enix tree:
  * `dep --help` ALREADY names the direction: "Arg order is needer-THEN-prereq; reversing wires the DAG
    backwards. Fix a backwards edge with `trk undep`."
  * `dep` ALREADY echoes the resulting sentence on success ("01M0PT61C now needs 01M0PSPWH"), so a
    reversal is visible to anyone reading the output.

VERIFIED AT HEAD (not relayed from the originating finding, which is from 2026-07-21 and predates
several trk upgrades):
    trk edit --help  |  grep --rm-doc  ->  0 hits.  There is no removal flag.
Confirmed still-live. The originating symptom: `trk edit <id> --add-doc <bad-id>` permanently attaches
a doc-ref; `--rm-doc` is an unknown flag. A typo'd or placeholder doc id (e.g. "none") becomes a
permanent cosmetic doc-ref. Harmless in effect -- it points nowhere -- but uneditable except by a raw
log edit, which is exactly the operation the tool's own consumers are told never to perform.

THE INCONSISTENCY IS INTERNAL, which is what makes it a defect rather than a wish:
    --add-tag / --rm-tag     PAIRED
    dep       / undep        PAIRED (and `dep --help` explicitly points at undep as the fix)
    doc set   / doc unset    PAIRED (01KXC1TY7, landed)
    --add-doc / (nothing)    UNPAIRED   <-- this issue
    --body    / (nothing)    UNPAIRED   <-- 01M0QJ8K4, now ruled
The tool has already decided, four times, that a mutation gets an inverse. Two escaped.

NOTE the distinction from 01KXC1TY7, which is DONE and is a different verb: `trk doc unset` removes a
doc_id -> path REGISTRATION. This is about removing a doc-REF from a TASK. Registering correctly does
not help a task that already carries a bad ref.

PROPOSED: `--rm-doc <doc_id>` on `trk edit`, mirroring `--rm-tag` exactly (tombstoned, union-merge-safe,
same as the existing removal verbs). If a doc-ref should be immutable by design, say so in `edit --help`
and the recovery guidance -- but silence plus an unknown-flag error reads as an oversight, and the
consumer's only remaining route is the forbidden one.

WORTH AUDITING WHILE IN THERE: whether any other mutation is one-directional. The two found here were
found by asking the question, not by hitting them -- 01M0QJ8K4 cost six task bodies before anyone asked.

RESOLVED 2026-08-23. `--rm-doc <doc_id>` added to `trk edit`, backed by a new
`undocref` event. It mirrors `untag`'s fold shape (plain list removal, no tombstone map) rather than
`undep`/`unin`'s: a docref is a per-TASK attribute, and under the disjoint-writer rule two lanes never edit
the same task, so only a single lane's own append order matters — which a union merge preserves within each
side. An EDGE needs the tombstone map precisely because it can be authored from either endpoint and so
genuinely can be raced. Matching is by doc_id alone (a `#section` suffix is accepted and ignored), so one
removal clears every section ref to that doc; an absent ref reports "(no such ref; no-op)" rather than
silently reading as a removal.

AUDIT REQUESTED IN THIS ISSUE — DONE, and it is now clean. Every mutation checked for an inverse:
  --add-tag / --rm-tag        PAIRED
  --add-doc / --rm-doc        PAIRED  <- this issue
  dep / undep                 PAIRED (and now direction-explicit, 01M0QKHWQ)
  in / unin                   PAIRED
  arc / arc --undo            PAIRED
  arc --standing / --undo     PAIRED
  doc set / doc unset         PAIRED
  --replace-body/--append-body  PAIRED (01M0QJ8K4)
  state <s>                   BIDIRECTIONAL by construction (any state -> any state, incl. un-archiving
                              via `trk state <id> done`)
  --title, --priority         single-direction by nature — a scalar replace has only one meaning
                              (`--priority 0` already restores the default rank)
No one-directional mutation remains.

Filed 2026-08-23 from the Enix side, where trk is used heavily by agents. Scott's suggestion, and the
evidence for it is stronger than "it would be convenient".

## THE GAP

`trk edit <id> --body` REPLACES. There is no append. So the universal operation "add a note to this
task" is a hand-built read-modify-write performed by the CALLER, in shell, every time.

## WHY THAT IS THE WRONG PLACE FOR IT -- the load-bearing argument

**Only trk can read its own body correctly.** The current body is the merge of `log.jsonl`'s setBody
events AND `snapshot.jsonl` -- `trk compact` writes a full-state snapshot and TRUNCATES the log, so a
body last written before the most recent compact lives in the snapshot and NOWHERE ELSE. Every
external append helper has to reimplement that merge, and there is a recorded instance of one getting
it wrong destructively: a helper scanning only `log.jsonl` for the last setBody returned "0 existing
chars" for such a task, the caller wrote existing+addition, and the task lost its ENTIRE original
body. It hit TWICE in one session (Enix rows 01KVKJ1EN, 01KXMMVK5).

An append verb deletes the reconstruction step. The tool already knows how to read its own state; the
caller does not, and cannot be expected to.

## MEASURED HISTORY -- six instances, seven weeks, all one root cause

  2026-07-03  backticks inside a double-quoted `--body` ran as SHELL; the stored body had HOLES where
              the backticked words were.
  2026-08-07  the compact/snapshot case above -- helper reported "0 existing", caller TRUNCATED. x2.
  2026-08-13  a shell-substituted "old body + append" with a silent `|| echo ''` fallback WIPED a
              row's whole diagnosis trail (Enix 01KZY98VM); recovered only because the old text
              happened to still be in the agent's context.
  2026-08-20  compact/merge silently dropped a live task's most-recent setBody (01KZTV44M) -- adjacent
              cause, same blast radius, and the recovery was again a hand re-apply of extracted bytes.
  2026-08-21  two separate "re-verified, appended" commits on 01KZ3BW22 wrote BYTE-IDENTICAL bodies.
              Zero durable signal added, no error, no warning. The task kept getting re-worked
              because each pass silently overwrote the last.
  (+ this repo's own 01M0EM10X: "an agent lost a multi-paragraph body to this".)

Two of trk's own issues have ALREADY been closed against symptoms of this gap -- 01KXC1TY5 added
`show --body` as "a raw body read path for safe edit round-trips", and 01M0EM10X made `--body -` read
stdin instead of storing the literal "-". Both made the MANUAL round-trip safer. Neither removed the
need to do it manually, and the losses continued after both landed. That is the argument for fixing
the primitive rather than the third symptom.

Corroborating signal on frequency: the consuming project documents the workaround in THREE separate
runbooks and ships a shim script (`scripts/trk-note.sh`) whose entire purpose is to wrap this. A
one-off does not get written into three runbooks.

## PROPOSED SHAPE (not prescriptive -- the maintainer's call)

1. **`trk note <id> <text>`** (or `trk append`) -- read the current body via trk's own state merge,
   append, write. Accepts `-` for stdin like `--body` now does, so long text needs no shell quoting.
   Optionally a separator convention (blank line, or a `--sep` flag).
2. **Keep `--body` as REPLACE**, unchanged and explicit. The two operations are genuinely different
   and both are wanted; the bug is that only one is spellable.
3. **Consider making a byte-identical setBody loud** -- a warning, or a `--allow-noop`. That is the
   2026-08-21 case: the write "succeeded" while adding nothing, and the silence is what let it repeat.
4. Possibly `--body-file <path>` as a third spelling, since agents already stage bodies in files to
   dodge shell quoting.

## WHY IT MATTERS DISPROPORTIONATELY HERE

trk's value is accumulated context -- a task body that grows a diagnosis trail across sessions is the
whole point of an append-only tracker. This gap attacks exactly that: every loss above destroyed
accumulated reasoning, and the 2026-08-21 case destroyed it invisibly, so the task read as
"investigated twice" while holding one pass's worth of content. A tracker whose append operation can
silently truncate is failing at its defining job.

## REFINEMENT (Scott, 2026-08-23): there should be NO DEFAULT — make both explicit

Scott's proposal on reading the above: rather than adding an append verb alongside `--body`, drop the
default entirely — `--replace-body` and `--append-body`, each explicit, neither implied.

**This is not a new convention. It is trk's OWN convention, applied to the one flag that escaped it.**
`trk edit --help` at HEAD:

    trk edit <id> [--title <s>] [--body <s>] [--add-tag <t> ...] [--rm-tag <t> ...]
            [--add-doc <doc_id[#section]> ...] [--priority <n>]

`--add-tag` / `--rm-tag` / `--add-doc` all REFUSE a default: the caller must name the direction. Only
`--body` implies one — and it implies the DESTRUCTIVE one. The inconsistency runs in exactly the wrong
direction, because a lost tag is trivially recoverable and a lost body is the six losses tabulated
above. The tool already decided that a mutation with two directions must name its direction; body
edits were simply never brought under that rule.

Restated as the mandate this project applies to its own kernel APIs: `--body` is a footgun whose
spelling looks innocent. Splitting it makes the destructive operation UNSPELLABLE BY ACCIDENT, which
is a stronger fix than any amount of documentation — and this issue's own history is the evidence,
since the workaround is already documented in three runbooks plus a shim script and the losses
continued anyway.

### One addition, and it is the load-bearing half of the migration

**REMOVE `--body` outright; do not deprecate it.** A deprecation that still performs the replace
preserves the exact failure mode for every existing caller — the warning scrolls past in an agent's
tool output and the body is gone regardless. Removing it converts every wrong call site into a LOUD
argument-parser error, which is the only migration that actually repairs callers rather than
annotating them.

Note trk already has a deprecation precedent and it is instructive by contrast: `--add-tag arc:<slug>`
is "still honored, but warns". That is correct THERE, because the legacy behaviour is harmless — the
tag lands, just via the old spelling. Honor-with-warning is the wrong instrument here, where honoring
the old spelling IS the bug.

The blast radius is small and known: the consuming project's `scripts/trk-note.sh`, three runbook
mentions, and agent prompts — all mechanical, all one-time, all better fixed loudly than left to fail
silently one more time.

### Consequent shape

    trk edit <id> --replace-body <s|->     explicit, destructive, says so
    trk edit <id> --append-body  <s|->     explicit, additive; reads the current body via trk's own
                                           log+snapshot merge, which is the half no external caller
                                           can do correctly (see the 2026-08-07 truncation above)
    --body                                 REMOVED (hard error naming both replacements)

Both accept `-` for stdin, as `--body` does today, so long text needs no shell quoting. The
byte-identical-write warning proposed above applies to `--replace-body` specifically — that is where
the 2026-08-21 silent no-op occurred.

## RULED (Scott, 2026-08-23) — both open points decided; do not re-litigate

The two items above were raised as recommendations. Scott has ruled on both. They are DECIDED, not
proposals, and an implementer should treat them as constraints:

1. **`--body` is REMOVED, not deprecated.** A hard argument-parser error naming both replacements.
   Rejected explicitly: honor-with-warning, because the warning scrolls past in an agent's tool output
   while the body is destroyed anyway — the deprecation would preserve the exact failure this issue
   exists to end. (Contrast the tool's existing `--add-tag arc:<slug>` deprecation, which is correctly
   honor-with-warning BECAUSE its legacy behaviour is harmless.)

2. **The byte-identical-write warning belongs on `--replace-body` ONLY**, not on both verbs. That is
   where the 2026-08-21 silent no-op occurred: an "append" that overwrote with near-identical text and
   added nothing, so a task read as investigated twice while holding one pass of content. An append
   that happens to produce no change is a different and far less interesting event, and warning on it
   would be noise.

### Migration, since removal makes it loud rather than optional

Known blast radius on the Enix side, all mechanical and one-time: `scripts/trk-note.sh` (whose entire
purpose is shimming this gap — it likely becomes a thin alias or is deleted), three runbook mentions
(the `fan-out` and `rec-bot` skills, and `CLAUDE.md`'s tracker section, all of which currently teach
the `trk show <id> --body | trk edit <id> --body -` round-trip), and agent prompt boilerplate that
repeats the same warning. Every one of those gets SIMPLER after the change rather than more complex —
the round-trip instruction disappears entirely, replaced by one verb.

### Sequencing note

NOT implemented at filing time, deliberately: a Fable agent was mid-flight using `trk` heavily to
build tasks from the teeth audit, and changing the CLI under a running consumer would break it. This
is a small, well-specified change with no dependency on anything else — it can land whenever the
tracker is quiet.

IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-23, exactly as RULED — no re-litigation.
  * `--body` REMOVED from `trk edit`: a hard argument-parser error naming both replacements. Not deprecated.
  * `--replace-body <s|->` and `--append-body <s|->`, both explicit, neither implied. Both take `-` for stdin.
  * `--append-body` reads the current body through trk's own log+snapshot fold — the half no external caller
    can do correctly. Covered by a test that compacts first (so the body lives ONLY in snapshot.jsonl, and the
    test asserts the string is absent from log.jsonl), then appends: this is the 2026-08-07 truncation shape.
  * Separator: exactly one blank line between the old body and the new text, normalized so pre-existing
    trailing newlines don't stack. No separator when the body is empty. No --sep flag (not ruled; the
    convention is enough).
  * Byte-identical warning scoped to `--replace-body` ONLY, per ruling 2. A no-op append is silent.

SCOPE NOTE: `trk add --body` and `trk show --body` KEEP that spelling. Creation has nothing to replace and
show's is a READ flag — neither is a two-direction mutation, so the rule this issue establishes does not
reach them. Every semantic of the old `--body -` (one-newline trim, refuse-on-no-stdin, refuse-on-empty) is
unchanged and now applies to both new flags.

MIGRATION on the Enix side is now loud, as intended: `scripts/trk-note.sh` (likely deletable — its whole
purpose was shimming this), the fan-out and rec-bot skills, and CLAUDE.md's tracker section all teach the
`trk show <id> --body | trk edit <id> --body -` round-trip. Every one of them gets SIMPLER: the round-trip
instruction disappears, replaced by `trk edit <id> --append-body`.

Filed 2026-08-23 from the Enix side. Third of the explicit-direction family, with 01M0QJ8K4 (body
replace/append, RULED) and 01M0QK1C4 (--add-doc has no inverse).

THE SHAPE. `trk dep A B` means "A needs B". Both arguments are bare positionals of the same type, so
reversing them produces a VALID edge pointing the wrong way — the DAG is wrong, the ready frontier is
wrong, and nothing errors.

PROPOSED: `trk dep <id> --needs <id>`, and `trk undep <id> --needs <id>` to match. ONE positional, ONE
flagged. The asymmetry is the mechanism: you cannot SWAP two things when only one of them is spellable
positionally, so a reversal stops being a typo and becomes a sentence you would have to write
backwards deliberately. It also reads as one: `trk dep 01ABC --needs 01XYZ`.

REJECTED ALTERNATIVES, so they are not re-proposed:
  * BOTH flagged (`--needer X --prereq Y`) — order-independent, but you still have to know which word
    means which, so it moves the confusion from position to vocabulary rather than removing it. And
    "needer" is not a word anyone reaches for.
  * INFIX keyword (`trk dep A needs B`) — reads best of the three, but it is an unusual CLI shape,
    undiscoverable from --help conventions, and inconsistent with trk's otherwise flag-based surface
    (--add-tag, --rm-tag, --priority).

MIGRATION: hard-error the bare two-positional form rather than accepting both, on the same reasoning
Scott ruled for 01M0QJ8K4 — a tolerated legacy spelling keeps the footgun, and here the blast radius is
small and known (CLAUDE.md's tracker section, a few runbook lines, agent prompt boilerplate).

=== SEVERITY, STATED HONESTLY — this is POLISH, not a defect, and should rank BELOW 01M0QJ8K4 and
01M0QK25Q ===

Unlike the body-append gap, this one is well-mitigated at HEAD and I could find no measured instance in
the Enix tree:
  * `dep --help` ALREADY names the direction: "Arg order is needer-THEN-prereq; reversing wires the DAG
    backwards. Fix a backwards edge with `trk undep`."
  * `dep` ALREADY echoes the resulting sentence on success ("01M0PT61C now needs 01M0PSPWH"), so a
    reversal is visible to anyone reading the output.
  * It is RECOVERABLE — `undep` exists, is tombstoned and union-merge-safe, and `dep --help` points at
    it by name.
Contrast 01M0QJ8K4: silent, destructive, six measured body losses across seven weeks, with the
workaround documented in three runbooks and failing anyway.

he recalls agents getting the direction wrong SEVERAL TIMES — plausibly before the upgrade that added
the direction note to `dep --help`, which would explain why the tree carries no recent incident. So the
mitigations above are probably WHY it stopped, not evidence it was never a problem. That reframes the
proposal from "a footgun nobody has hit" to "a footgun that was hit repeatedly and is currently held
shut by documentation" — and documentation-as-the-only-guard is precisely what the other two issues in
this family are about.

Residual risk is narrow and agent-shaped: you must reverse the args AND not read the echo. Agents are

Scott's disposition: file it as extra insurance; he expects to land the CLI upgrades together anyway,
so the marginal cost of including it is near zero.

IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-23. `trk dep <needer> --needs <prereq>` and
`trk undep <needer> --needs <prereq>`; the bare two-positional form hard-errors with a message that prints
the corrected command back. Both rejected alternatives stayed rejected.

ONE ADDITION beyond the filed proposal: `--needs` is REPEATABLE (`trk dep A --needs B --needs C`), matching
`trk add --needs <id> ...` which already worked that way. Wiring several prerequisites is one thought, not N
commands, and repeats cannot reintroduce the ambiguity — the needer is still the only positional.

Landed together with 01M0QJ8K4 and 01M0QK1C4 as Scott expected, so the marginal cost was indeed near zero.

Filed 2026-08-23 from the Enix side, where the workaround is documented in two runbooks and has still
cost a measured loss.

VERIFIED AT HEAD: `trk archive --help` mentions nothing about decisions or open questions (grep for
decision/open question -> 0 hits). The behaviour is as designed; the hazard is that the design has a
sharp edge nobody is warned about at the point of use.

THE HAZARD. `archive` graduates the done queue to the changelog and flips each task to `archived`,
which is a TOMBSTONE hidden from every view. A task body, however, routinely accumulates more than the
work: a "FIX NOTE", an open fork, a "this part is Scott's call", an OPEN QUESTION. The WORK was done --
the task is legitimately closeable -- but the DECISION was never that task's scope, and archiving takes
it out of sight along with the tombstone.

MEASURED: on 2026-08-12 a publish-cadence fork was archived out of sight this way and recovered only by
accident while someone wrote a handoff. The consuming project now carries the mitigation in two
runbooks as a manual pre-archive step: grep the done queue's bodies for `scott-decision` / `OPEN
QUESTION` / `FIX NOTE` / `your call` and `trk add` each as a standalone task BEFORE archiving. That
mitigation is prose, it fires only if the operator remembers, and it is duplicated in two places --
the same shape as 01M0QJ8K4's three-runbook workaround, which kept failing until the primitive changed.

WHY THE TOOL IS THE RIGHT PLACE. `archive` already walks every body it is about to graduate -- it emits
a changelog bullet per task. It is the only actor that sees the full done queue at the moment of
burial, and it is the only one that can act before the tombstone hides the text.

PROPOSED SHAPES, unweighed:
  (a) `archive` scans each closing body for a configurable marker set (default: `scott-decision`,
      `OPEN QUESTION`, `FIX NOTE`, `your call`, `TODO`) and WARNS, listing task id + matched line, so
      the operator can split them out first. Non-blocking; the warning is the whole value.
  (b) as (a) but REFUSES without `--allow-buried-decisions`, on the grounds that this is a data-loss
      class and a warning in a long archive run scrolls past (the same argument that ruled hard-removal
      over deprecation on 01M0QJ8K4).
  (c) `archive --dry-run` -- which already exists and previews the queue -- additionally reports the
      marker hits, making the existing preview step sufficient without changing archive's own contract.

(c) is the cheapest and composes with the existing workflow; (b) is the strongest if this is judged a
data-loss class rather than an ergonomics one. Maintainer's call.

NOT A BUG in the merge/tombstone model -- `archived` hiding from every view is correct and deliberate.
This is about what rides along with it.

IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-23. Scott RULED shape (b) — REFUSE, not warn — with the
FULL proposed marker list including TODO.
  * `archive` scans every closing body and refuses with a nonzero exit, listing `<short-id> [marker] <line>`.
  * `--allow-buried-decisions` is the deliberate override; it still REPORTS, and says it is archiving anyway
    rather than the preview's 'a real run would refuse'.
  * `--dry-run` reports the hits WITHOUT refusing — a preview buries nothing, so shape (c) is folded in for
    free rather than being an alternative to (b).
  * Markers: scott-decision, OPEN QUESTION, FIX NOTE, your call, TODO. Matched CASE-INSENSITIVELY — a body
    written by a human or an agent will not match a configured casing reliably, so the guard must not depend
    on shouting.
  * Configurable via .tracker/config.json -> archive.decision_markers (JSON array of strings). An explicitly
    EMPTY array disables the check, and is deliberately distinct from an ABSENT key (= use the defaults): an
    opt-out has to be spellable, and it has to differ from saying nothing.

KNOWN CONSEQUENCE, accepted with the ruling: TODO is common in ordinary work notes, so this WILL fire often.
That is the cost of the stronger guard Scott chose; the config key is the release valve for a repo that finds
the default too noisy, and narrowing the list is a one-line config edit.

title: trk add: an unrecognised flag is reported by blaming the TITLE -- `--tags=a,b` yields "unknown flag '<the title>'", pointing at the one argument that is correct
body:
FOUND 2026-09-01 in live use on the Enix tracker; reproduced deliberately afterwards.

    $ trk add --tags=a,b "Fixture title that should not be blamed"
    trk: unknown flag 'Fixture title that should not be blamed'

The unknown flag is `--tags=a,b` (the correct spelling is `--tag <t>`, repeatable). The title is a
perfectly well-formed positional and is the ONE argument in the line that is right. The parser
evidently swallowed `--tags=a,b` into the title slot, then met the real title as an unexpected second
positional and reported THAT as a flag.

COST, and it is the reason this is worth fixing rather than shrugging at: the message sends you to
inspect your title. Mine was long, contained backticks and an em dash, and had been written through a
shell heredoc -- so I spent a cycle hunting a quoting bug in an argument that was never the problem,
before noticing the flag name. A message that named `--tags=a,b` would have cost seconds.

FIX SHAPES, either would do:
  * report the ARGUMENT THAT FAILED TO PARSE, not the one that arrived unexpectedly afterwards; or
  * when an unknown token begins with `--`, say so explicitly and, if a near-match exists among the
    known flags, name it -- `--tags` -> `--tag` is a one-character edit distance and the plural is the
    natural guess for a repeatable flag.
The second is strictly better here: the whole class of error is someone reaching for the plural of a
repeatable option.

RELATED SHAPE, same session, not the same bug: `--tags=` is also a plausible spelling because several
OTHER trk flags do take `=`-joined values. Worth a look at whether the repeatable flags are
discoverable as repeatable from `--help` alone.

title: next/list --json omit the BODY, so the mechanical full-frontier triage a fan-out mandates cannot be scripted -- and the markers that decide a task's bucket live only in the body, at its tail
body:
FOUND 2026-09-01 while triaging a 280-task ready frontier for an away fan-out.

    trk next --json | python3 -c "...print(sorted(d[0].keys()))"
    ['id', 'priority', 'seq', 'short', 'state', 'tags', 'title']

No `body`. Same for `trk list --json`.

WHY IT BITES rather than being a nice-to-have. Enix's fan-out skill REQUIRES a mechanical triage of
EVERY ready task before an orchestrator may claim the autonomous work is exhausted -- explicitly "the
WHOLE list, scripted over tags + title keywords, not the top N, not a sample". The discriminators that
decide which bucket a task lands in are `HOLD`, `DEFER`, `RULED`, `scott-decision`, "NOT resolved",
"your call" -- and the skill is emphatic that these are APPENDED, so they sit at the END of a long
body while the opening paragraphs still read like ordinary buildable work. Every one of those signals
is invisible to `--json`.

The practical result on 280 tasks: tags and titles were scriptable, and everything else needed a
`trk show` per candidate. That is precisely the step where I repeatedly found tasks whose work was
already done, already ruled, or blocked on someone else -- the expensive discovery the triage exists
to make cheap.

TRK ALREADY HAS THE BODY IN HAND at that moment: `trk next --help` says its search terms match "over
title+body+tags", so the filter reads the body and the emitter drops it.

FIX SHAPES:
  * simplest -- include `body` in `--json` unconditionally. The consumer is a machine; size is not the
    concern it would be for the human view.
  * if size IS a concern (a 3 MB render is not hypothetical here), a `--json-full` / `--with-body`
    flag, or a `--body-tail <n>` emitting the last n lines, which is where the markers actually are.
  * cheapest useful subset if neither appeals: a boolean per task for whether the body matches any of
    the decision markers, so a triage script can at least SEE which rows need a `show`.

WORTH DECIDING rather than defaulting: the third option encodes Enix's marker vocabulary into trk,
which is arguably the wrong layer. The first keeps trk generic and pushes the grep to the caller. I
would take the first.

title: compact GCs a task that NON-TRACKER files cite by id, destroying the provenance of a decision recorded outside the tracker -- four scenarios/registry.tsv rows now cite ids that resolve to nothing
body:
FOUND 2026-09-01 on the Enix tracker, by a lane resolving registry rows held on dead ids.

THE INSTANCE. `scenarios/registry.tsv` has an `in-par` column whose value 3 REQUIRES a `held` column
naming the task that owns that row's first verification run. Four rows -- TOOLCONFERTEST,
TOOLLAUNCHTEST, RING3I2CHID, RING3USBMOUSE -- cite ids (01KYTDVC7, 01KYSWDSN, 01KZV686M) that now
resolve to nothing.

THEY ARE NOT TYPOS, and establishing that is what makes this a trk issue rather than an Enix one:
`git log -S` finds all three cited in the very commits that landed their rows (b0fc533f, d4a5a455,
78121bef). They were real tasks, honestly cited. `compact` physically GCs archived/dropped tasks, so
the record is simply gone.

WHY THAT IS WORSE THAN AN ARCHIVED ID. Seven sibling rows in the same audit were resolved by READING
the archived owner's body and seeing whether a verification had actually happened -- three were
cleared on the strength of a recorded PASS, four got fresh owners because their bodies showed a
feature landing with no boot. For a GC'd id there is no body to read, so "verified, write-back
forgotten" is indistinguishable from "never booted" and the only honest state is the unverified one
the rows already carry. A week of gate-governance provenance was destroyed silently.

THE DESIGN GAP. trk's compaction rules were written about task-to-task references -- `needs` edges,
arcs, citations inside other task bodies, all of which trk can see. They say nothing about ids cited
from files OUTSIDE the tracker, which trk cannot see and which are, in this project, load-bearing:
a registry column, a source comment, a design doc, a commit message.

SHAPES, none obviously right, which is why this is filed rather than fixed:
  * a pre-compact WARNING listing ids about to be GC'd, so a caller can grep its own tree first. Cheap,
    keeps trk ignorant of its consumers, puts the check where the knowledge is. Probably the answer.
  * an opt-in "cited externally" pin (a tag, or a config-listed glob trk greps before compacting).
    More capable, more coupling.
  * tombstones -- keep id + title + final state forever, GC only the body. Answers "did this exist and
    what was it" without unbounded growth, which is exactly the question a dangling citation asks.
  * rule it a caller responsibility and say so in design.md, so the next person hits documentation
    instead of a mystery.

RELATED, not the same: `dangling-tracker-id-lint.sh` on the Enix side checks id EXISTENCE and its own
selftest asserts that a citation of a COMPACTED/ARCHIVED id PASSES -- deliberately, so archival does
not redden a tree. That is a defensible rule for archived ids and it is why nothing caught these.

title: Live lease state: 'claimed' becomes 'this task is taken' (hides it from next), and today's commit-tied completion report is renamed 'submitted' -- legacy serialized 'claimed' must keep decoding as submitted
body:
RULED (Scott, 2026-09-14, in an Enix session): trk gets a LIVE LEASE meaning "this task is taken", and the
names move to match ordinary ticket usage:
  * `claimed` -- NEW meaning: the lease. Written when work is handed out, so `next` stops offering a task
    someone already has. Not next-eligible; does not satisfy a prereq (the work is not done).
  * `submitted` -- today's `claimed`, renamed with its semantics unchanged: "the commit I'm riding completes
    this task, pending verification". Not next-eligible, does not satisfy a prereq, counts as remaining in
    render, is the awaiting-verification queue (`list --state submitted`), promoted to done or demoted to
    open by the post-gate reconcile.
Lifecycle: open -> claimed -> submitted -> done, with claimed -> open as the release.

WHY: in Enix fan-outs the only thing stopping two lanes or two concurrent sessions from starting the same
task is the orchestrator's memory. Scott read `claimed` as exactly this lease; the current meaning is closer
to "submitted", so the rename fixes the vocabulary rather than adding a near-synonym beside it.

WHERE EACH IS WRITTEN (context for the design, decided on the Enix side): the lease is a fact true whether
or not a lane's work ever merges, so it is written to the MAIN checkout's store and is visible to every
tree immediately. `submitted` is true only if the lane's commit lands, so it is written in the lane's
worktree and travels with the commit via merge=union. The Enix consumer is an MCP front end for trk
(Enix task 01M29TMPQ, which needs this) taking a required tree selector per call.

CONSTRAINTS:
  1. EXISTING LOGS MEAN COMPLETION. Every serialized `"state":"claimed"` already written (Enix alone holds
     109 across log.jsonl + snapshot.jsonl) means submitted, and so will any written by a pre-rename binary
     on a long-lived branch that union-merges in later. They must decode as submitted forever. Reusing the
     wire token "claimed" for the lease makes those lines ambiguous; one structural answer is to never
     reuse it -- the legacy token decodes to submitted, and the lease gets a wire token that has never
     meant anything else. Choose and record the encoding in design.md.
  2. OLD HABIT HAZARD. Agents and docs have written `trk state <id> claimed` to mean completion for months.
     After the rename that same command silently takes a lease: the task drops out of the
     awaiting-verification queue and nobody verifies it. Make the habitual misuse fail loud where the
     state machine allows it -- e.g. claimed -> claimed refused with a hint naming `submitted` -- and say
     in design.md what is and is not caught.
  3. A LEASE NEEDS A RELEASE PATH. A lane that dies or is abandoned must not strand its task as claimed
     forever. Candidates: an explicit release verb/sweep, expiry, a recorded holder (lane/worktree name +
     ts) that a sweep can check. This is a design fork -- bring a recommendation back to Scott before
     building it.
  4. Every surface that names the state moves together: model.zig State + its predicates, json_codec,
     render markers (the lease and submitted need distinct markers; say which keeps `[c]`), `list --state`,
     `stale`'s exclusion (a submitted task keeps being excluded; decide and record whether a leased one is),
     help text, design.md's state list and Settled rulings, README, and the tests.

VERIFICATION: host tests here (`zig build test`); then the Enix orchestrator verifies against the Enix
store (the 109 legacy values fold as submitted; a lease set in main hides the task from `trk next`) and
updates Enix's CLAUDE.md, fan-out/save-sweep skills and issue-tracker.md in the adopting commit (Enix task
01M2GG485).

title: trk mcp-serve: expose the verb table as MCP tools over stdio, so masked exits, shell-executed backticks, swapped positionals and direction-less body edits are unrepresentable -- every tool takes a required tree selector because subagents share the session's one server
body:
`trk mcp-serve`: trk speaks MCP (JSON-RPC 2.0, newline-delimited, over stdio) so an agent calls typed tools
instead of shelling out. Filed from the Enix side, where it is task 01M29TMPQ in arc 01M29TM00 (trk, enixedit
and enixnet-zig all getting MCP front ends). The Enix task keeps the adoption half: registering the server,
moving CLAUDE.md and the skills, and verifying against the Enix store.

WHY -- every item is a recorded incident on the Enix tracker, not a hypothesis. Each is a SHELL failure that
a typed tool call makes unrepresentable rather than discouraged:
  * MASKED EXITS. `trk state <id> done | tail -1` reports tail's exit; an orchestrator did it on nearly every
    close in one session (2026-09-11). A tool result has no pipe.
  * BACKTICKS EXECUTING AS SHELL inside `--body`/`--append-body` text. Bodies are exactly where code
    identifiers and shell snippets belong, so this is the highest-traffic hazard.
  * SWAPPED POSITIONALS -- the reason `dep` refuses the two-positional form. Named parameters make the swap
    unrepresentable.
  * A BODY EDIT WITH NO DIRECTION -- as a required enum (append | replace) it cannot be omitted, and the
    destructive one is named at every call site.
  * VERB SCOPE. `archive`/`compact`/`render` are orchestrator-only, and a lane ran `render` anyway because
    the rule lived in prose it never read.

SHAPE
  * `trk mcp-serve`: initialize (declare the tools capability), tools/list, tools/call; ignore id-less
    notifications. Stdout carries protocol only; diagnostics go to stderr. std-only, like the rest of trk.
  * The tool schema is DERIVED FROM THE SAME VERB TABLE `main` dispatches on, so CLI and MCP cannot drift.
    Every tool calls the same code the CLI verb calls -- never a reimplementation. Bodies in particular
    must go through trk's own snapshot+log fold: a caller reading log.jsonl directly sees a body last
    written before the newest compact as EMPTY and truncates it.
  * Read verbs (show, list, next, tree, log) return structured JSON content, not formatted text -- which
    also removes the reason anyone pipes them.
  * States in the schema are the post-rename ones (01M2GGFGR): `submitted` is the completion report;
    `claimed` requires a holder; release is its own tool.
  * The CLI stays the primary surface -- docs cite it, humans use it, it works over ssh. MCP is an
    additional front end. A change that deprecates CLI verbs has overstepped.

TREE SELECTION -- the constraint that shapes every tool (ruled by Scott, 2026-09-14: expose it as an option)
  Measured: Claude Code spawns a stdio MCP server ONCE PER SESSION from .mcp.json, cwd = the session's repo
  root, and SUBAGENTS share that one process (they run inside the parent session and multiplex over its
  pipe). So a lane working in a git worktree reaches a server whose cwd is the MAIN checkout, and trk's
  walk-up discovery would silently retarget every lane write from its worktree's .tracker/ to main's.
  Therefore every tool takes a REQUIRED `tree` parameter: "main", or a worktree path. No default -- same
  named-at-the-call-site argument as the body direction. A path that is not a linked worktree of the
  server's repo is REFUSED, never silently resolved elsewhere (trk already recognizes a linked worktree by
  its `.git` FILE; how to validate membership without shelling out to git is the builder's call -- record
  it in design.md).
  Which tree a write belongs in turns on one question: is the fact true only if the lane's commit lands?
    * yes -> the worktree: `submitted`, and edits describing what the lane's change did.
    * no  -> main: the `claimed` lease and its release, and defects/follow-ons a lane discovers (filed in
      a worktree they die with an abandoned lane).
  The server enforces only the tree's validity, not this policy; the policy is the caller's, stated per call.

VERB SCOPE -- note for the design, not a settled shape
  Because subagents share the session's one server, the server cannot tell an orchestrator's call from a
  lane's, so hiding `archive`/`compact`/`render` cannot be done server-side by caller. What can scope it:
  per-agent-type tool allowlists on the Claude Code side (an agent definition names the MCP tools it gets),
  which needs those verbs to be separate tools rather than one generic `trk` tool with a verb argument.
  So: one MCP tool per verb.

  * The Enix arc 01M29TM00 recommends each tool serving MCP itself (this task's shape) over one external
    wrapper that shells out to all three tools; that recommendation is recorded there but not yet ruled.
  * Whether the stdio JSON-RPC loop is written as a small helper the other two Zig tools (enixedit,
    enixnet-zig) can reuse, since the arc calls for all three.

title: log append is an UNLOCKED length-then-pwrite: 24 concurrent adds lost 18 events AND corrupted the log into 'failed to load store: NotAnObject'
body:
MEASURED 2026-09-18 on a throwaway store. 24 concurrent `trk add` calls -> 5 log lines, 6 of 24 titles surviving, and ONE LINE HOLDING TWO CONCATENATED JSON OBJECTS. `trk list` on the result: `trk: failed to load store: NotAnObject`. Not a degraded read, not one lost task -- THE WHOLE STORE FAILS TO LOAD. Every consumer goes with it: the CLI, the MCP server every agent writes through, make lint's dangling-tracker-id check, and `render`'s TODO.md projection.

ROOT CAUSE, read from source not inferred -- trk/src/store.zig:1731 `persistAppend`:
    var f = try sub.createFile(self.io, log_name, .{ .read = true, .truncate = false });
    const end = try f.length(self.io);
    try f.writePositionalAll(self.io, line.items, end);
That is LENGTH-THEN-PWRITE: a read-modify-write with no lock. Two writers both read `end = N` and both pwrite at N; the second overwrites the first, and if the two lines differ in length the survivor keeps a tail of the loser -- which is exactly how one line ends up holding two objects. Confirmed absent by search: no flock, no LOCK_EX, no O_APPEND, no advisory lock anywhere in trk/src (`grep -rn "flock|LOCK_EX|lockFile|O_APPEND|append_mode" ~/dev/zig/trk/src/` -> zero hits).

THIS FALSIFIES A DOCUMENTED DESIGN PREMISE. CLAUDE.md states: "the log is append-only with a `merge=union` driver *precisely* so agents can write in parallel -- so `add`/`edit`/`dep`/`in` and `state` `submitted` are open to subagents." merge=union is a GIT-MERGE driver: it reconciles two divergent COPIES of the file. It does nothing for two processes writing ONE file in one working tree, which is the case the parallel-write permission actually creates.

AND THE PRESCRIBED FAN-OUT PATTERN AIMS EVERY LANE AT ONE FILE. issue-tracker.md / the fan-out skill rule that a defect or follow-on a lane DISCOVERS goes to `tree: "main"` -- deliberately, so an abandoned lane cannot take it down. Correct for durability, and it means N concurrent lanes all append to the MAIN checkout's single log. The worktree isolation that separates their code changes gives no separation here at all.

CURRENT STATE OF THE REAL STORE: CLEAN. 2927 log lines and 1486 snapshot lines, 0 unparseable, checked the same day. Nothing has been lost yet that this can detect -- but a silently dropped event leaves no trace by construction, so "0 unparseable" bounds the CORRUPTION, not the LOSS.

THE FIX, and there is a proven precedent in this repo from the same day: wrap the read-length-then-write in an exclusive advisory lock over a sibling lockfile, exactly as scripts/verdict-ledger.sh's recordRow() was fixed this morning (same defect shape -- unlocked read-modify-write -- proven with a 24-concurrent-writer selftest arm that now requires all 24 rows to survive). Either:
  (a) flock(LOCK_EX) held across length+pwrite+sync. Also protects against a git checkout/merge rewriting the file underneath a writer, which the orchestrator does routinely (merge-lane.sh auto-commits main's dirty log before every lane merge).
  (b) open with O_APPEND and a single write(), letting the kernel make offset-selection atomic. Simpler, but does not cover the git-rewrite race, and leaves the fold's other callers unprotected.
(a) is the better match for the failure modes actually observed here. WHICHEVER IS CHOSEN, IT SHIPS WITH A CONCURRENCY ARM: N writers, all N events present and every line parseable -- the arm is the point, since this bug is invisible to every existing test (they are all single-writer).

REPRODUCER, 30 seconds, no repo state touched: `mkdir ~/trk-race && cd ~/trk-race && trk init`, then 24 backgrounded `trk add "race-probe-$i"` with a `wait`, then count `grep -o 'race-probe-[0-9]*' .tracker/log.jsonl | sort -u | wc -l` and run `trk list`.

title: trk archive has refused for two consecutive sessions and the done queue is 36 deep: the decision-marker guard's false positives are dominated by tasks that quote the markers BECAUSE the markers are their subject -- including the tasks that built the guard
body:
OBSERVED across two consecutive sessions (2026-08-28 and 2026-08-29 save-sweeps): `trk archive`
refuses, the done queue does not graduate, and nothing reaches docs/CHANGELOG.md. The queue is now
36 tasks deep.

THE REFUSAL IS WORKING AS DESIGNED and should not be weakened casually -- `archived` is hidden from
every view, so burying an unresolved fork with a finished task is a real loss, which is exactly why
the guard exists. The problem is its FALSE POSITIVE RATE on one specific shape.

`trk archive --dry-run` reports 37 marker hits, and the guard labels most of them "(prose-shaped)".
Reading them, the dominant class is SELF-REFERENTIAL: tasks whose bodies quote the marker strings
BECAUSE THE MARKERS ARE THEIR SUBJECT. Concretely, from the dry-run:
  * 01M12D4EV -- four hits, all from its own body explaining which markers the guard matches
    ("The other markers (scott-decision, OPEN QUESTION, FIX NOTE, your call) are ... none of them
    collide with a filename shape the way TODO does").
  * 01M12ZG5E -- six hits, its body literally saying it "necessarily quotes `[TODO]`,
    `[OPEN QUESTION]` and `[scott-decision]` because those markers ARE its subject".
  * 01M135SJX / 01M135SK1 -- hits from ENUMERATING sibling task ids and their tags in a findings
    roll-up ("01M138E21 (HIGH, scott-decision)").
  * 01M1650PW -- the scott-decision tagging pass itself, whose body cannot describe its own job
    without naming the tag, and whose last sentence is "It resolves nothing."
So the tasks that BUILT AND FIXED the marker guard are the ones the marker guard now refuses to
archive, and a roll-up task is blocked by naming its children's tags.

WHY IT COMPOUNDS RATHER THAN SITTING STILL: every session that files a roll-up, an audit summary, or
any work ABOUT the decision-marker mechanism adds another permanently-stuck entry. The queue only
grows, and the escape (--allow-buried-decisions) is all-or-nothing across the whole run -- so using it
to clear five genuine false positives also waves through any REAL buried fork in the other 31, which
is precisely the loss the guard exists to prevent. That all-or-nothing shape is what has made me
decline twice: at the end of a long session, auditing 36 bodies to earn one blanket override is not a
thing to do tired, and doing it untired is still the wrong shape.

FIX SHAPES (unweighed -- and this is a guard-semantics call, so it is Scott's):
  (a) Per-task escape: --allow-buried-decisions=<id,id,...>, so an operator clears the specific
      false positives they actually read and the guard still protects the rest. Smallest change,
      keeps the guard's teeth, makes the override auditable in the shell history.
  (b) Teach the guard the self-referential shape -- e.g. ignore a marker inside backticks or inside
      a quoted span, which is how every false positive above is written. Riskier: a real fork could
      be quoted too.
  (c) Exempt by tag: a task tagged as tracker/tooling work ABOUT the marker mechanism is expected to
      quote markers. Narrow, but relies on tagging discipline the guard cannot verify.
(a) is the one I would reach for, because it does not require the guard to get any smarter and it
leaves a record of exactly which bodies a human cleared.

RELATED, already filed: 01M13JXWN (a count-PRESERVING body edit defeats archive's per-task count
assertion) is a different defect in the same command; worth looking at together since both are about
what archive trusts.


REC-BOT 2026-08-30 :: OPTIONS: (a) per-task escape `--allow-buried-decisions=<id,...>`; (b) teach the
guard the self-referential shape (ignore a marker inside backticks or a quoted span); (c) exempt by tag ::
NEW: (d) the guard ALREADY makes the distinction the fix needs, and nobody has used it. Its own dry-run
output labels every hit `(prose-shaped)` or `(marker-shaped)`, and I measured the split at HEAD: of 40
hits, 37 are prose-shaped and 3 are marker-shaped. So narrowing the REFUSAL to marker-shaped hits --
while still REPORTING the prose-shaped ones -- would unblock the queue today, keep the guard's teeth on
the class it was built for, and require no new flag, no new tagging discipline, and no quoting heuristic.
The classifier is already there; only the refusal predicate reads it too broadly ::
EVIDENCE:
- `trk archive --dry-run 2>&1 | tail -1` -> "  (40 line(s); a real run without --allow-buried-decisions would refuse)"
- `trk archive --dry-run 2>&1 | grep -c 'marker-shaped'` -> 3
- `trk archive --dry-run 2>&1 | grep -c 'prose-shaped'` -> 37
- dry-run output: "  01M12ZG5E  [scott-decision] (prose-shaped)  necessarily quotes `[TODO]`, `[OPEN QUESTION]` and `[scott-decision]` because those markers ARE its"
- dry-run output: "  01M1650PW  [scott-decision] (prose-shaped)  Scott, 2026-08-29: the scott-decision tag has been applied inconsistently. ... It resolves nothing."
- dry-run output: "  01M135SJX  [scott-decision] (prose-shaped)  01M138CEN (HIGH), 01M138DCV (HIGH), 01M138E21 (HIGH, scott-decision), 01M138EGN, 01M138F95, 01M138FMZ."
- dry-run output: "  01M12ZG5E  [OPEN QUESTION] (marker-shaped)  genuine \"OPEN QUESTION:\" to that same task, archive again -- the old code let it through" -- one of the 3 marker-shaped hits is itself a self-referential quote in a task ABOUT the guard, so even the narrow class is not clean
- `trk list --state done | wc -l` -> 62 (the body reported 36; the queue has grown, so the compounding claim is measured, not predicted)
- `trk show 01M13JXWN | sed -n '2p'` -> the sibling defect ("trk archive's per-task count assertion is defeated by a count-PRESERVING body edit"), state open, untagged
:: WEIGHING: the body's framing is right on every count -- the refusal is working as designed, the escape's
all-or-nothing shape is what makes it unusable at a session end, and the false-positive class is dominated
by tasks whose SUBJECT is the markers. The measured split turns that qualitative reading into a number and
the number is decisive: 37 of 40 are the class the guard should not be refusing on, and the queue has grown
from 36 to 62 since filing, so the compounding claim is now measured rather than predicted.
Weighing the four: (a) is the body's own lean and it is genuinely good -- it keeps the teeth, makes the
override auditable, and requires the operator to have READ each body they clear. Its cost is that it does
not reduce the reading burden at all; it just makes the burden per-task instead of all-or-nothing, and the
body's own reason for declining twice was that "auditing 36 bodies to earn one blanket override is not a
thing to do tired". At 62, per-task clearing is 62 decisions instead of one, which is more auditable and
more work -- a real improvement in safety, not in usability.
(b) is the riskiest: a genuine fork CAN be written inside backticks, and the guard exists precisely
because burying one is unrecoverable (`archived` is hidden from every view). Do not weaken the match.
(c) relies on tagging discipline the guard cannot verify, which the body says and is right about.
(d) dominates (a) on usability without giving up what (a) protects, because the split is not a heuristic
the guard would have to learn -- it is a classification the guard already computes and prints. And it
degrades safely: a prose-shaped hit is still REPORTED, so an operator reading the dry-run still sees every
one; only the refusal stops firing on them. The residual risk is the one the dry-run itself shows -- even
the marker-shaped class contains a self-referential quote (01M12ZG5E's) -- so (d) is not a clean
separation and should be paired with (a) as the escape for the remainder. Three per-task overrides is a
tractable session-end action in a way that 62 is not.
The principle underneath is one this batch keeps hitting: `docs/debugging.md` rule 5's spirit is that a
check must be able to fail AND that something must act on it. A check that fires so broadly that it is
never acted on has failed the second half -- and the observed behaviour (two consecutive sessions
declining, queue growing) is that failure happening. `agent-first.md`'s harness section is the positive
statement: these tools are load-bearing agent-first surfaces because "an agent parses [their verdicts] by
name, not prose it eyeballs" -- and the guard's own `(prose-shaped)`/`(marker-shaped)` label is exactly
such a parseable verdict that nothing currently consumes.
:: SELF-REFUTE: the strongest fact against (d) is that the prose/marker classifier might be a heuristic
with its own false NEGATIVES -- if a genuinely buried fork can be written in a form the classifier calls
prose-shaped, then narrowing the refusal to marker-shaped hits lets exactly the loss the guard exists to
prevent through the door. I read the dry-run's labels and counted them, but I did NOT read trk's
classifier implementation to see how it decides between the two (it lives in the sibling trk repo, outside
this tree). That read is mandatory before (d) ships, and if the classifier is weak, (a) alone is the
answer.
:: REC: (d) paired with (a), contingent on reading trk's prose/marker classifier first (see SELF-REFUTE).
Narrow the REFUSAL to marker-shaped hits while still reporting prose-shaped ones -- that alone drops the
blocking set from 40 to 3 on today's queue -- and add the per-task `--allow-buried-decisions=<id,...>`
escape for the remainder, so the three that still block are cleared by an operator who read them, with the
override visible in shell history. Do NOT take (b): a genuine fork can be written inside backticks, and
weakening the match trades an unusable guard for an unsafe one. Look at 01M13JXWN in the same pass as the
body suggests -- both are about what archive trusts, and both are currently untagged/unowned in a way that
lets the queue grow. High confidence in the ranking; the guard-semantics call itself stays Scott's.
:: DISPOSITION: proposed


THE FIX FOR THIS EXISTS BUT IS NOT INSTALLED YET (2026-08-31). A lane landed both trk defects in the
sibling repo (~/dev/zig/trk commit 45db249, NOT pushed, NOT installed). The live ~/.local/bin/trk is
still the 2026-08-28 00:20 binary and therefore still has both bugs — verified by mtime, and the lane
was explicitly fenced off from installing over it because this session and five sibling lanes were
using it concurrently.

WHAT CHANGED, and it is a better answer than the one this task was going to get: the per-task escape
no longer asserts a COUNT. A count is defeated by a count-PRESERVING edit (delete one marker-shaped
line, append another), and so is any finer sub-count, one shape over. The exemption now asserts the
hit set's IDENTITY: `--allow-buried-decisions-for <id>:<n>:<digest>`, digest = FNV-1a/32 over the
matched lines in body order (Cli.hitDigest, src/cli.zig:1930). The count survives only for legibility
— both must match, so they cannot disagree dangerously, and `15 -> 16` is a diagnosis where a hash
mismatch is only a verdict. The old `<id>:<n>` form is now a hard error rather than a silent
downgrade to the weaker guarantee.

OPERATIONAL RULE FOR WHENEVER THIS QUEUE IS FINALLY DRAINED — read this before pasting any digest.
finding-20260803005917: "a lane's COMPUTED derived value (hash, pinned id, checksum) is stale on
arrival if anything changed its derivation"; the rule that predicts it exactly is that a derived value
survives iff its own input set was untouched by everything that landed meanwhile. A digest here is
computed over a TASK BODY, and task bodies are exactly what every fan-out lane appends to — this
session alone has five lanes appending right now, and any one of them can add a marker-shaped line to
a task in the archive queue. So: NEVER carry a digest across a merge, a wave, or a session. Recompute
it at the moment of the archive run, from the guard's own printed `<id>:<n>:<digest>` line, which is
why the lane made `--refuse`/`--dry-run` print the paste-ready form under each unexempted task.
Treat any digest written down anywhere — including one written above — as a cross-check, never a
source.

NOT the finding-20260728182455 trap, checked rather than assumed: that one is about a derived short
identifier that must be STABLE for life being silently rewritten by compaction. Here invalidation on
content change is the entire mechanism, so churn is the feature, not the bug. The two look alike and
are opposites.

WHAT REMAINS ON THIS TASK: the queue is 62 deep and still blocked, because the tool that would unblock
it is built but not rolled out. Rollout is orchestrator-owned and deliberately deferred out of a live
wave. 01M13JXWN and 01M13JXWS stay `claimed` for the same reason — closing them would let `trk archive`
graduate them into the CHANGELOG while the binary everyone runs still carries both bugs.

title: Make a landed ruling remove its own #scott-decision tag: pick the mechanism (a trk rule verb that appends+untags atomically, a lint that fails on a tagged task whose body carries a RULED marker, or splitting the decision from its carrier task at ruling time)
body:
Scott 2026-09-11, on being handed an already-answered question: 'it is insane that this is a new task as a scott-decision that asks to remove a scott-decision that should have already been removed... I feel like this is abusing the task system.' Measured the same day: 01M1WWQSC carried three of his rulings in its body (09-07 x2, 09-09) and still read as open; 01M1ZKRWY and 01M1ZM8MM likewise; 11 stale tags came off in one day, and at least 3 had been surfaced to him repeatedly in the interim. Root cause is structural: 'trk edit --append-body' records the ruling and says nothing about the tag. Options, his pick: (1) a 'trk rule <id> <text>' verb that appends the ruling and removes the tag in one step, so the tag cannot be forgotten -- strongest, needs a trk release (sibling repo ../trk); (2) a lint in make unit-fast that FAILS on any open task tagged scott-decision whose body contains a ruling marker (RULED/Scott ruled/RULED BY SCOTT -- note the phrasings differ, so the matcher needs care) -- cheapest, catches it after the fact; (3) split the decision task from its build carrier at ruling time, so the tag leaves with the closed decision. The doctrine itself is already recorded in issue-tracker.md's Settled rulings; this task is the mechanism only.

SECOND HALF, same complaint: the end-of-turn 'OPEN -- needs you' block re-listed ALL pending decisions every turn (CLAUDE.md mandates the block, not its contents), so Scott saw the same 8-12 items dozens of times in one session and asked 'is this any different from the 20 other times I've been asked about it'. A stale tag made it worse: an answered question kept reappearing. title: tombstones --rebuild recovers title + end-state but NOT arc memberships (all 2521 back-filled records carry "arcs":[]), so trk tree's compacted-members block is empty for everything compacted before the index existed -- the two fixes compose only for FUTURE compacts
body:
MEASURED 2026-09-16 on the Enix store, immediately after installing the binary carrying 01M2M2K1J
(the tombstone index) and 01M29P5T7 (`tree` reports compacted members) and running the one-time
`trk tombstones --rebuild`.

THE MEASUREMENT, not an inference:
  wc -l .tracker/tombstones.jsonl            2521
  grep -c '"arcs":\[\]'  tombstones.jsonl    2521   <- every record
  grep -c '"arcs":\["'   tombstones.jsonl       0   <- none carry a membership
And the consequence, on the very arc whose misreading motivated 01M29P5T7:
  trk tree 01M0JN18R   renders its live and `[a]` archived members correctly, and prints NO
                       "compacted members (N)" block at all.

WHY. `compact` writes a tombstone at the moment the task is collected, when its arc memberships are
still in the store, so it records them -- correct, and it is why the feature works going FORWARD.
`--rebuild` instead scans `git log --all -p -- .tracker/log.jsonl` and reconstructs each id's title and
end-of-life state from its `add` / `setTitle` / `setState` events. It does not reconstruct `in` edges,
so every back-filled record is membership-less by construction.

THIS CONTRADICTS A STATED EXPECTATION, which is why it is filed rather than shrugged at. 01M29P5T7's
lane wrote, as the first thing for the orchestrator to check after installing: "if the D1-D5 members
were compacted BEFORE 01M2M2K1J's index existed, the block will be empty until you run
`trk tombstones --rebuild`". The rebuild does not fill it. A reader following that note would conclude
the install failed, or that the arc genuinely had no compacted members -- which is the exact wrong
inference 01M29P5T7 exists to prevent, one layer up.

SO, TODAY, THE SPLIT IS: `trk show <compacted id>` answers fully for the whole of history (exit 2 with
title and end-state -- verified on 01M1RQ7XK, 01M0QJWJ7 and 01M1ZNBY2). `trk tree <arc>` answers only
for tasks compacted from here on.

FIXABLE, and probably cheaply: the `in` edges ARE in the scanned history -- `in` events live in the
same `log.jsonl` the rebuild already reads end to end. The rebuild reconstructs three event kinds; this
asks it to reconstruct a fourth and populate `arcs`. Worth checking whether an `unin` can appear after
an `in` (in which case the same largest-`ts` fold the state recovery uses applies), and whether
reachability-derived membership -- which `dep` can create as a side effect -- needs the same treatment
or is deliberately out of scope for a tombstone.

Until then, `tree`'s block should probably SAY that it only covers post-index compactions rather than
rendering an unqualified empty, since an absent block currently means either "no compacted members" or
"compacted before the index existed" and those are the two readings this whole line of work exists to
separate.
